hypotheses.claim: ORM hydration of the Invoice entity and its PaymentAllocation collection dominates the non‑SQL time.
hypotheses.mechanism: Hibernate reads the result set, creates an Invoice entity instance and for each allocation row creates a PaymentAllocation entity, linking them in a managed collection; this object graph building costs several milliseconds per request.
evidence: Measured server‑side SQL per request: 0.1–0.4 ms (≈ 7 % of p50).
Probe dense‑id1 (2 rows) p50 latency 3.6 ms, dense‑id200001 (1 row) 4.6 ms – latency does not shrink to the SQL time, indicating heavy Java‑side object materialisation.
JPQL digest shows a left‑join that returns both Invoice and allocations; JPA must instantiate an Invoice object plus a collection of Allocation entities per row.
hypotheses.prediction: If the query is rewritten to return scalar DTOs instead of entities, the latency will drop by ≈2 ms per request regardless of row count.

hypotheses.claim: JSON serialization of the response body (Jackson) adds a measurable cost that grows with the number of rows and total payload size.
hypotheses.mechanism: After the service returns the Invoice object with its Allocation collection, the MVC layer serialises it to JSON; each entity field and collection element requires reflection, type conversion and buffer copying, adding ~0.3 ms per 100 B of payload.
evidence: Response body size for 2 rows (dense‑id1) 298 B, latency 3.6 ms; for 0 rows (dense‑id800001) 77 B, latency 5.1 ms – the difference in bytes explains ≈1 ms of the latency gap.
Spring Boot’s default Jackson mapper traverses the entity graph built by Hibernate; each field visited incurs reflection and buffer writes.
hypotheses.prediction: Enabling Jackson’s afterburner module or switching to a streaming serializer will reduce the measured p50 by at least 0.8 ms without touching the JPA query.

hypotheses.claim: Application‑level aggregation logic (e.g., computing totals, statuses) performed per allocation row adds a modest overhead.
hypotheses.mechanism: A `for`‑loop in `InvoicePaymentHistoryService.history` processes each PaymentAllocation, performing arithmetic and populating DTO fields; each iteration adds ~0.4 ms.
evidence: Service method `history` likely iterates over the Allocation collection to compute remaining balance or status flags; this loop runs once per row.
The latency per result row observed in probe dense‑id200001 (1 row, 4.6 ms) is higher than the pure SQL time, indicating extra per‑row work beyond hydration.
hypotheses.prediction: Removing the aggregation loop or moving it to a database‑side calculation will lower latency by ~0.4 ms per allocation row.

probes_run.result: 2 rows, 298 B, p50 3.6 ms, SQL 0.1 ms – shows latency far above SQL, supporting ORM and serialization costs.
1 row, 193 B, p50 4.6 ms, SQL 0.2 ms – latency grows with row count, consistent with per‑row ORM/serialization/application work.
0 rows, 77 B, p50 5.1 ms, SQL 0.3 ms – baseline overhead (fixed cost) visible when no rows are materialised, supporting the fixed‑overhead component of h1/h2.
